title: Sidepane priority layers and failover matrix — notes & prototypes
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures an exploration of an alternative console navigation pattern for the Redwood Console: an adaptive sidepane composed of stacked priority layers with explicit failover routing rules. The goal is to reduce surface complexity for first-time users while preserving fast access for power users and making routing and fallback behavior explicit for platform and SRE flows (rollouts, model variants, dedicated vs hosted routing).

Problem statement / observations: 
- The existing left rail has grown organically (many entry points). New users get overwhelmed; power users complain about deep click paths for specific operational routes (traces, model variants, tenant routing).
- Product routes conflate two orthogonal axes: task (what you want to do: deploy, monitor, debug) and operational scope (customer, model, region). This leads to duplicated entry points and stale shortcuts.
- Runbook and SRE tasks frequently need to change routing based on capacity or tier (if Dedicated pool is saturated show Hosted fallback). Current navigation hides these rules.
- We lack a lightweight way to expose current routing/failover state without an extra page. Engineers often open multiple tabs and ping the API to confirm which route a request will take.

Design goals / constraints: 
1) Prioritize tasks over views: show task-first entry points (Create inference endpoint, Run eval, View latency spike) with context scoping available as a second step.
2) Make routing policies discoverable: expose the effective routing for a task as a small inline state chip in the sidepane.
3) Allow quick switch: power users need keyboard shortcuts and one-click deep links into model / route combos.
4) Non-breaking: keep current URLs stable where possible; implement progressive enhancement behind a feature flag.
5) Surface-only changes first: initial implementation should be UI-only wiring to show states without changing backend behavior.

Proposal: Sidepane as stacked priority layers
- Layer 0 (Top): Global actions — create new resource, quick search, CLI snippet. Minimal height, always pinned.
- Layer 1: Task palette — top 6 tasks derived from telemetry per-org (defaults: New endpoint, Live debug, Eval run, Embeddings batch, Rollout policy, Cost analyzer). Each task has: name, 1-line description, default route, routing chip.
- Layer 2: Scope selectors — customer/tenant pickers, model selector, region selector. These are collapsible and remember last-used values per user.
- Layer 3: Operational views — traces, metrics, logs, persisted requests. These are contextualized by the current scope.
- Layer 4 (Footer): Quick links & admin panels — secrets, billing, quota.

Routing chip model (inline state)
- Each task tile shows a compact chip: e.g. [Dedicated pool: eu-west-1 > primary] or [Hosted fallback]. Chip color indicates expected latency/cost tier (green/amber/red). Hover shows full failover matrix: primary -> secondary -> fallback with capabilities (supports streaming/embeddings/quantized).
- The chip is populated from a new read-only endpoint (UI-only shim for prototype) that returns the effective route for the current org + task + scope.

Wireframe variations (sketch notes):
Variant A — Minimal stacked tiles
- Visual: compact tiles, 6 tasks visible, chips to the right. Scope row collapsed to a single line below tasks. Keyboard: number shortcuts 1..6 mapped to tasks.
- Use case: onboarding and demos (keeps cognitive load low).
- Tradeoffs: deeper clicks to reach model variant pages.

Variant B — Scoped-first hybrid
- Visual: Scope selector expanded by default for users who regularly operate at model-level. Tasks are a second column.
- Use case: ML engineers and SREs who need immediate context.
- Tradeoffs: Slightly larger sidepane; can be collapsed to Variant A via toggle.

Variant C — Power rail (dense)
- Visual: Compact list with icons, inline route chips displayed for every item. Supports multi-select scopes and pinned task combos.
- Use case: on-call and platform teams.
- Tradeoffs: higher visual density; not great for new users.

Accessibility notes:
- Keyboard nav: tasks reachable via numbers; scope pickers via Ctrl+K quick open. ARIA roles for the stacked regions.
- Contrast: chips must meet WCAG AA for color states.

Failover matrix example (sketch):
- For 'Run inference' task, failover sequence for org AcmeCorp: Dedicated eu-west-1 (supports streaming) -> Dedicated us-central-1 (no streaming) -> Hosted streaming-enabled. The chip shows 'Dedicated eu-west-1' with amber hue (expected 60–120ms). Hover shows full matrix with capability flags.

Backlog / implementation plan (MVP -> v1):
- MVP (UI-only, feature-flagged, 2 sprints): implement Layer 0–2, task tiles, scope picker, chip with stubbed data; keyboard shortcuts; telemetry to capture task usage.
- v1 (3–6 sprints): integrate with routing metadata API, hover panels showing capability flags, deep-linking per task+scope, admin toggle for defaults per org.
- v2+: predictive task ordering (ML model on telemetry), inline routing controls for toggling fallback priorities (admins only), A/B test to measure task discovery time.

Open questions & decisions needed:
- Where does the role-based access control (RBAC) plane live for task tiles? Some tasks should be hidden for certain roles (billing, secrets). Decision: tile-level ACL or scope-level?
- Should the routing chip be actionable (allow switching fallback order) or read-only in UI v1? Recommendation: read-only initially, editable in v2 behind admin path.
- Performance: adding the chip means an extra read to resolve effective route. Cache granularity? per-org + per-task with 1m TTL recommended.
- URL model: clicking a task should deep link to /console/task/:taskId?scope=... Keep legacy routes for existing links. Need router mapping table.

Usability metrics to track post-launch:
- Task discovery time (time from login to first successful task completion).
- Click depth for power workflows (median clicks to open model variant page).
- On-call runbook success rate (how often users select correct route without checking API).
- Feature flag adoption and toggle rates.

Work items (short tickets to create):
- CON-1482: prototype UI-only stacked sidepane (Priya)
- CON-1483: scope picker component and remember-last-used (Eun-Ji)
- JIRA-3247: routing chip hover panel design and copy (Marco)
- INF-2021: routing metadata read endpoint (backend stub)

Design appendix (notes for visual designer):
- Iconography: use task-first pictograms not product-area icons (e.g., lightning bolt for Live debug, funnel for Eval run).
- Microcopy: chips should use short names and unify region format (region-code > pool-name).
- Animation: collapse/expand of layers should be snappy (120–180ms) and respect reduced-motion preference.

Immediate next steps:
1) Align with Erik (SRE) on visible capability flags and what to include in hover matrix.
2) Create low-fidelity mocks for Variant A/B and test with 6 internal users (mix of PM/engineer/SRE) next week.
3) Spin up a backend stub for routing metadata so the UI prototype can show realistic chips (INF-2021).

Notes-to-self / freeform fragments: 
- Consider a tiny persisted "last task" quick-link in top-right when opening a tenant page.
- Could use the onboarding tour to teach the chip concept.
- If we add admin-editable fallbacks later, need audit trail (who changed fallback order, when).

End of note.

Feedback welcome — Priya (pri.menon@redwood.ai)
